This report ranks SIPNET parameters by their contribution to the variance of modeled
soil carbon and N₂O-N flux at 100 California cropland design points from 2016 to 2023.
Methane results are reported for the 11 design points with at least one recorded rice
season. Each result is a parameter's share of modeled parameter
variance at a design point, conditional on the current parameter priors.

## Background

A parameter matters for prediction when the model is sensitive to it and its value is
uncertain. The analysis combines the two, following the PEcAn variance decomposition
([LeBauer et al., 2013](references.html); [Dietze et al., 2014](references.html)).

SIPNET is run with every parameter at its prior median, then with each parameter moved
in turn to the 2.3, 15.9, 84.1, and 97.7 percentiles of its prior, all others at their
median. A spline through the five outputs gives the response to that parameter, and the
variance of the prior propagated through the spline is its contribution to the output
variance. The share of parameter variance is that contribution over the sum across all
plant and soil parameters at the design point. A parameter is treated as influential
where its share exceeds 5 percent, the criterion Fer et al. (2018) used to select SIPNET
parameters for calibration ([Fer et al., 2018](references.html)).

![Design points, colored by the PFT they were run under, with the number of design points in brackets. Outlines are the Cal-Adapt climate regions.](figures/site_map.png){#fig-map width=70% fig-align="center" .lightbox fig-alt="Map of California with 100 design points colored by plant functional type."}

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| Model | SIPNET 2.2.0, nitrogen cycle and anaerobic processes on |
| Design points | 100: 67 woody perennial, 14 row crop, 6 grass, 4 alfalfa, 3 rice, 2 corn, 4 uncropped |
| Period | 2016 to 2023, reported as the mean over the period |
| Parameters | 34 per cropped design point (21 plant, 13 soil), 13 per uncropped design point |
| Priors | PFT priors of the statewide inventory runs |
| Meteorology, initial conditions, management | member 1 of each inventory ensemble |
| Model runs | 13,364 |

## Share of parameter variance

![Prior uncertainty (CV), sensitivity (elasticity), and share of parameter variance. Points are medians across design points and bars span the interquartile range.](figures/variance_components.png){#fig-components width=100% fig-align="center" .lightbox fig-alt="Dot plot of coefficient of variation, elasticity, and share of parameter variance for the influential parameters of soil carbon and modeled N2O-N flux."}

| Output | Parameter | Median share (%) | Range (%) | Design points over 5 percent |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Soil carbon | Soil respiration Q10 | 62 | 4 to 78 | 99 |
| | Base soil respiration rate (0 °C, saturated soil) | 28 | 2 to 42 | 98 |
| Modeled N₂O-N flux | Soil respiration Q10 | 46 | 17 to 81 | 100 |
| | Nitrogen volatilization rate constant | 40 | 15 to 67 | 100 |
| | Nitrogen leaching fraction | 8 | 0 to 20 | 76 |

: Share of parameter variance across the 100 design points, for parameters with a median share above 5 percent. {#tbl-shares}

Two soil parameters account for most of the parameter variance in soil carbon, and
raising either lowers soil carbon at all 100 design points. A plant parameter exceeds 5
percent of the soil carbon variance at 19 of the 96 cropped design points, 18 of them
woody perennial, and at none for modeled N₂O-N flux.

## Variation across design points and PFTs

![Share of parameter variance, shown separately for soil carbon and modeled N₂O-N flux. Upper panels show the distribution across design points; green marks show the mean. Each lower bar is the average share among design points assigned to that plant functional type (PFT), not a contribution from the PFT itself.](figures/share_by_pft.png){#fig-pft width=100% fig-align="center" .lightbox fig-alt="For soil carbon and modeled N2O-N flux, upper boxplots show parameter shares across design points; lower bars show the average share within each plant functional type."}

The two parameters with the largest mean share for soil carbon and modeled N₂O-N
flux are the same in every plant functional type.

## Methane at sites with rice history

The methane analysis includes 11 design points with at least one recorded rice season
during 2016–2023. Plant functional type labels and irrigation events do not establish
crop history. The figure shows the two parameters that exceed the 5 percent screening
threshold at any of these design points.

![Share of methane parameter variance across 11 design points with recorded rice seasons. Points represent design points; boxes show the median and interquartile range. The dashed line marks the 5 percent screening threshold.](figures/methane_oat_parameter_shares.png){#fig-methane-oat width=85% fig-align="center" .lightbox fig-alt="Soil methane rate accounts for about 90 to 100 percent of methane parameter variance across 11 design points with rice history; soil respiration Q10 accounts for 0 to 10 percent."}

The soil methane rate accounts for a median 94 percent of methane parameter variance
(range 90–100 percent). Soil respiration Q10 accounts for a median 5.7 percent
(range 0–10 percent) and exceeds the screening threshold at eight design points.
These shares describe sensitivity under the current priors, not parameter
identifiability or agreement with observed methane. A reliable global variance
partition is not available for methane.

## Reporting scope

Shares are reported for soil carbon and modeled N₂O-N flux at
all 100 design points, and for methane at the 11 design points with recorded rice
seasons. Six other outputs were also computed. Plant carbon is low in these runs, with
net primary productivity below 20 g C m^-2^ yr^-1^ at the median design point of every
PFT; shares for these outputs are not presented.

## Interpretation

These are model-derived results. Parameters are drawn from priors that have not been
updated with observations, so each share depends on the prior widths; the prior for the
soil respiration Q10 is uniform from 1.4 to 5.0.

Each parameter is varied with all others at their medians, so the shares divide the sum
of single-parameter contributions and do not include interactions
([Saltelli et al., 2019](references.html)). Meteorology, initial conditions, and
management are held at one ensemble member; the global sensitivity analysis compares
those inputs with the parameters.

See [References](references.html) for the cited sources.
